clinical.body: This dorsal intrinsic extensor receives deep fibular motor supply, unlike plantar intrinsic muscles. Interpret toe movement alongside the long extensors rather than as an isolated EDB test.

pathology.body: Deep fibular motor dysfunction can affect the short dorsal extensor. The reference surface cannot establish the cause, severity or level of a neurological lesion.

ct.body: CT locates the dorsolateral calcaneal origin and adjacent foot bones, but is not the preferred test of this small muscle. Attenuation alone does not define a deep-fibular nerve lesion. This source lacks separately validated hallux-brevis anatomy.

mri.body: MRI can show dorsal-foot soft tissues near the short extensor origin when a focused injury question remains after radiography. Signal alone does not localise a nerve lesion. This selection does not separately identify extensor hallucis brevis.

xray.body: Foot radiographs show dorsolateral bone alignment and possible osseous injury near the muscle origin. They do not directly image extensor digitorum brevis. A normal film cannot rule out a muscle or nerve problem.

ultrasound.body: Ultrasound can identify the superficial dorsal muscle belly lateral to the long extensor tendons. It can guide a focused soft-tissue assessment but does not establish individual distal slips from this mesh. A deep-fibular nerve diagnosis needs wider evaluation.

selfCheck.question: Does this source contain a separate selectable extensor hallucis brevis?
selfCheck.answer: No. Only the supplied EDB identity is bound here; an absent separate structure must not be inferred from another specimen.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Straightens toes 2–5 and assists ankle dorsiflexion.

attachments.proximal: Lateral tibial condyle, anterior fibula and adjacent interosseous membrane.
attachments.distal: Extensor apparatus of toes 2–5, continuing to their middle and distal phalanges.

extended.modelLimit: One supplied muscle surface, not separately validated distal tendon slips or a nerve territory. Its reference shape cannot show weakness, compartment pressure or a tendon tear.

clinical.body: Compare lesser-toe extension with ankle dorsiflexion and the wider motor/sensory pattern.

pathology.body: Weakness of the long toe extensors can accompany anterior-compartment muscle injury or dysfunction of their deep fibular motor supply.

ultrasound.body: Trace EDL across the anterior ankle, distinguishing it from EHL. Follow the tendon course rather than identifying one cross-section; this specimen does not validate individual distal slips.

ct.body: CT identifies anterior-leg compartment relationships and associated bone injury. It does not routinely grade EDL muscle or tendon fibre injury. The single source surface does not validate four distal tendon slips.

mri.body: MRI can assess EDL muscle and tendon signal through the anterior leg and ankle. Trace it beside, rather than confuse it with, the hallux long extensor. This static model carries no strain grade or patient tendon finding.

xray.body: Leg and ankle radiographs assess bones and alignment around EDL. The muscle and its tendon continuity are not directly visible. A normal film does not explain isolated lesser-toe extension weakness.

selfCheck.question: Does weak lesser-toe extension identify one torn tendon?
selfCheck.answer: No. Compare ankle movement and the wider neurological pattern; this selection does not isolate individual tendon slips.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Straightens the great toe and assists ankle dorsiflexion.

attachments.proximal: Middle anterior fibula and adjacent interosseous membrane.
attachments.distal: Dorsal base of the hallux distal phalanx.

extended.modelLimit: The long hallux extensor is supplied as one surface. No tear, root lesion or separate distal attachment footprint is segmented; selecting it does not test L5 function.

clinical.body: Assess hallux extension alongside other dorsiflexors and the neurological examination.

pathology.body: Impaired great-toe extension may reflect local muscle/tendon injury or a neurological lesion.

ultrasound.body: Identify EHL among the anterior ankle tendons and follow its course, separating it from tibialis anterior and EDL. The static surface cannot establish tendon continuity in a patient.

ct.body: CT provides anterior-leg and ankle bone context along the EHL course. It does not directly establish a subtle tendon tear or L5 motor function. The long hallux extensor must remain distinct from EDL.

mri.body: MRI can follow EHL from its deep anterior-leg muscle belly toward the hallux tendon. Signal and continuity should be interpreted alongside the other anterior-compartment structures. This source cannot diagnose a root lesion or patient tear.

xray.body: Radiographs show associated tibial, fibular or foot bone injury, not EHL fibres. Dorsal hallux weakness with a normal film still requires clinical localisation. This mesh is no motor test.

selfCheck.question: Can this selection establish an L5 root lesion?
selfCheck.answer: No. It identifies a reference muscle, not the cause or distribution of weakness in a patient.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Bends toes 2–5; its tendons stop on the middle phalanges, unlike the long flexor.

attachments.proximal: Medial calcaneal tuberosity, plantar aponeurosis and septa.
attachments.distal: Middle phalanges of toes 2–5 through split tendons.

extended.modelLimit: This supplied short-flexor surface does not separately grade digital tendon slips, toe deformities or passive joint flexibility. Grouped bones are not validated digit-specific lesion labels.

clinical.body: The short flexor reaches the middle phalanges; the long flexor continues to the distal phalanges.

pathology.body: Lesser-toe deformity reflects the balance of muscles, tendons and joints, not simply shortening or rupture of the short flexor.

ct.body: CT shows plantar bone architecture and gross soft-tissue relationships around the short flexor. MRI more clearly separates small intrinsic muscles if their signal is the question. CT cannot validate this source as four individual tendon slips.

mri.body: MRI can distinguish the superficial central plantar FDB from deeper quadratus plantae. Its signal may be assessed with other plantar muscles, but one change does not define a digital tendon injury. The grouped foot bones give no patient toe-specific lesion labels.

xray.body: Weight-bearing foot radiographs can assess toe alignment and bony deformity. They do not directly reveal FDB tendon continuity or passive toe flexibility. A toe deformity should not be attributed to this single muscle from a film.

ultrasound.body: A plantar probe can image accessible FDB fibres and trace them toward the lesser toes. Deeper quadratus plantae and the long flexor lie in different layers and should not be conflated. This source does not resolve individual digital slips.

selfCheck.question: Can this grouped muscle prove that one digital tendon is ruptured?
selfCheck.answer: No. It is a reference surface with no separately validated pathological tendon slips.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Bends toes 2–5 and assists ankle plantarflexion.

attachments.proximal: Posterior tibial shaft below the soleal line.
attachments.distal: Plantar bases of the distal phalanges of toes 2–5.

extended.modelLimit: A supplied long-flexor surface is not four independently assessed distal tendon slips. The foot display does not validate individual pulley systems or tendon continuity.

clinical.body: Relate FDL to distal-joint flexion of toes 2–5, while recognising the combined action of long and intrinsic flexors.

pathology.body: Long toe-flexor injury or tibial motor dysfunction can alter active lesser-toe flexion.

ultrasound.body: Find FDL beside tibialis posterior behind the medial malleolus, then trace it distally. Distinguish adjacent vessels and nerve; this muscle selection is not a complete tarsal-tunnel examination.

ct.body: CT shows the posteromedial ankle bony tunnel and associated fracture anatomy. It is less direct for FDL tendon-sheath or fibre assessment than targeted ultrasound or MRI. Do not infer one of four distal slips from this whole surface.

mri.body: MRI follows FDL behind the medial malleolus and into the plantar foot alongside neighbouring flexors. It can assess tendon and sheath signal when clinically relevant. The display does not model a patient tarsal-tunnel lesion.

xray.body: Ankle and foot films assess bones adjacent to FDL, including medial-malleolar injury. They cannot directly show FDL tendon continuity. A normal film does not settle a focused posteromedial tendon question.

selfCheck.question: Does FDL stop at the middle phalanges like the short flexor?
selfCheck.answer: No. Its distal attachments reach the distal phalanges of toes 2–5; the short flexor reaches the middle phalanges.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Bends the great toe and assists ankle plantarflexion.

attachments.proximal: Distal posterior fibula and adjacent interosseous membrane.
attachments.distal: Plantar base of the hallux distal phalanx.

extended.modelLimit: The reference surface does not segment tenosynovitis, impingement, a tear or its sheath. Historical surgical-series findings are not prevalence estimates or a treatment pathway.

clinical.body: Posteromedial ankle symptoms with hallux movement may prompt assessment of the FHL tendon and its sheath.

pathology.body: FHL can develop tendon-sheath inflammation and tendon tears in dancers and nondancers.

ultrasound.body: Identify FHL between the posterior talar tubercles; great-toe movement helps confirm the tendon. Follow its course beneath the sustentaculum tali. Exploding this static surface does not reproduce tendon motion.

ct.body: CT defines posterior talar or sustentacular bone anatomy along the FHL route. It does not routinely diagnose tenosynovitis or demonstrate dynamic gliding. The reference muscle has no patient impingement sign.

mri.body: MRI can follow FHL through the posterior ankle and beneath the sustentaculum tali, assessing its tendon and sheath. Signal must be interpreted with symptoms and other posterior-ankle findings. Static separation of this mesh is not tendon motion.

xray.body: Ankle radiographs can reveal posterior talar bone variants or injury around the FHL course. They do not image the tendon fibres directly. A normal film cannot exclude a clinically suspected FHL disorder.

selfCheck.question: Is FHL tendon disease restricted to dancers?
selfCheck.answer: No. It has also been reported in nondancers; a selected clinical series cannot establish its population prevalence.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Plantarflexes the ankle and assists knee flexion; it crosses both joints.

attachments.proximal: Lateral aspect of the lateral femoral condylar region.
attachments.distal: Posterior calcaneus through the shared calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.

extended.modelLimit: Only the supplied lateral head is selected. Shared calf/Achilles context does not make a medial-head tennis-leg lesion a lateral-head diagnosis; no pathological head or tendon is modelled.

clinical.body: The two gastrocnemius heads contribute to plantar flexion through the shared Achilles apparatus and also cross the knee. Interpret this lateral-head selection within that shared anatomy.

pathology.body: An injured gastrocnemius muscle and a ruptured Achilles tendon are different lesions. A lateral-head reference surface does not establish which tissue accounts for calf pain.

ct.body: CT shows the lateral calf compartment and associated bone or deep soft-tissue context. MRI better characterises subtle lateral-head muscle injury. This selection is separate from the medial head and Achilles tendon.

mri.body: MRI can localise signal in the lateral gastrocnemius head and distinguish it from soleus or medial-head injury. Interpretation needs the wider calf and clinical history. The static source does not contain a strain grade.

xray.body: Knee and leg films survey nearby bone injury, not lateral-gastrocnemius fibres. A normal radiograph does not exclude muscle injury. Calf symptoms also require consideration beyond this head.

ultrasound.body: Ultrasound can inspect the superficial lateral head and its interface with deeper soleus during a focused calf examination. It should not be labelled a medial-head tennis-leg finding. A muscle view alone cannot assess venous causes of calf pain.

selfCheck.question: Is this lateral-head selection also a separate Achilles tendon selection?
selfCheck.answer: No. The reference head and supplied Achilles tendon retain distinct identities despite their shared functional apparatus.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Plantarflexes the ankle and assists knee flexion; it crosses both joints.

attachments.proximal: Posterior femur at the medial condylar region.
attachments.distal: Posterior calcaneus through the shared calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.

extended.modelLimit: Only the supplied medial head is selected. No strain, fluid collection or venous clot is rendered; source defects are not diagnostic findings and this is not a vascular scan.

clinical.body: Gastrocnemius crosses knee and ankle, whereas soleus does not. Both transmit force through the shared Achilles apparatus.

pathology.body: Gastrocnemius strains and Achilles tendon ruptures are distinct injuries. Medial gastrocnemius injury is a common explanation for the clinical label tennis leg.

ultrasound.body: Ultrasound can assess medial gastrocnemius injury and adjacent fluid. Calf pain also has non-muscular causes, including venous thrombosis; a muscle view alone does not exclude them.

ct.body: CT gives bony context around the medial calf, but a subtle muscle injury may require MRI for tissue characterisation. MRI studies separate medial-head injury from neighbouring soleus findings. This source surface does not represent a patient tear.

mri.body: MRI can localise a medial-head injury and distinguish it from deeper soleus change or fluid at their interface. The scan must be interpreted with clinical and vascular assessment where relevant. This model contains no patient strain or venous finding.

xray.body: Radiographs show knee or leg bone injury around the medial head, not the muscle fibres. A normal film cannot diagnose or exclude a calf strain. The source surface is anatomical context only.

selfCheck.question: Does selecting this muscle exclude a vascular cause of calf pain?
selfCheck.answer: No. The model is not a patient examination and does not evaluate veins or blood flow.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Extends and externally rotates the hip, helping raise the trunk from a flexed position.

attachments.proximal: Posterior ilium and sacrum, with associated lumbar fascia and sacrotuberous ligament.
attachments.distal: Iliotibial tract and femoral gluteal tuberosity.

extended.modelLimit: This supplied muscle has no denervation pattern, pressure lesion or patient-specific weakness. Its disappearance in dissection mode does not simulate inferior gluteal neuropathy.

clinical.body: Assess extension strength in the context of pain, other hip muscles and the wider neurological examination.

pathology.body: Inferior gluteal nerve dysfunction can reduce gluteus-maximus strength and hip extension.

ct.body: CT locates the bulky gluteus maximus in the superficial posterior buttock over the deep rotators. It can define a large collection or traumatic swelling and its relation to pelvic bone, while MRI is better for detailed muscle injury.

mri.body: MRI follows gluteus maximus from the posterior pelvis toward the iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity. Its broad superficial position distinguishes it from medius and minimus at the greater trochanter; focal abnormalities require actual image review.

xray.body: Pelvic and hip radiographs assess adjacent sacral, pelvic and proximal-femoral bone. They do not depict separate gluteus-maximus fibres or prove that a painful buttock is caused by this muscle.

ultrasound.body: Ultrasound can examine an accessible focal area of gluteus maximus superficial to the deep gluteal layer. Its thickness and wide attachment area limit complete sonographic coverage, particularly toward the deep pelvic margin.

selfCheck.question: Which named gluteal nerve is most directly associated with maximus motor supply?
selfCheck.answer: The inferior gluteal nerve. Weak hip extension still requires a broader assessment rather than diagnosis from one muscle selection.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Abducts the hip and helps keep the pelvis level over the supporting leg.

attachments.proximal: Outer ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines.
attachments.distal: Greater trochanter, principally its lateral and superolateral facets.

extended.modelLimit: This muscle surface does not separately map its tendon facets, tears or bursae. A group visibility change is not a Trendelenburg test or a simulated gait cycle.

clinical.body: Pain over the outer hip with side-lying or single-leg loading can involve the gluteal tendons. Location alone does not identify one injured tendon.

pathology.body: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome includes gluteal tendon disorders; it should not automatically be labelled isolated bursitis.

mri.body: MRI may help assess gluteal tendons when clinically needed; imaging is not required for every clinical diagnosis of gluteal tendinopathy.

ultrasound.body: Follow medius toward the greater trochanter in two planes; distinguish its more superficial muscle layer from the deeper minimus.

ct.body: CT places gluteus medius along the lateral ilium, deep to maximus posteriorly and superficial to minimus, approaching the greater trochanter. It can show major muscle bulk loss or a collection, but tendon and subtle fibre changes are better assessed with MRI or targeted ultrasound.

xray.body: Hip radiographs evaluate the greater trochanter and surrounding bone, including an attachment fragment if present. They do not directly resolve the medius tendon or distinguish it from minimus.

selfCheck.question: Does lateral hip pain prove that the trochanteric bursa is the only affected tissue?
selfCheck.answer: No. Gluteal tendon pathology can contribute; clinical assessment considers the surrounding tissues.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Abducts and stabilizes the hip; anterior fibres assist internal rotation.

attachments.proximal: Outer ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines.
attachments.distal: Anterior aspect of the greater trochanter.

extended.modelLimit: Minimus is independently selectable but its tendon and enthesis are not separate meshes. No labelled tear, perfusion map or clinical muscle-strength assessment is supplied.

clinical.body: Minimus tendon symptoms may overlap those of medius and hip-joint disease. A painful lateral hip is not a structure-specific diagnosis.

pathology.body: Gluteal tendinopathy and tendon tears may coexist with other hip pathology; the source surface cannot establish either condition.

mri.body: MRI can support assessment of the deep gluteal tendons when symptoms and examination require further investigation.

ultrasound.body: Minimus lies deep to medius; its tendon reaches the anterior greater-trochanteric facet. Do not swap these two tendon identities.

ct.body: CT locates gluteus minimus deep to medius on the lateral ilium as it approaches the anterior greater trochanter. Cross-sectional anatomy can orient a larger mass or collection, although MRI and targeted ultrasound better assess the abductor tendons.

xray.body: Hip radiographs assess the greater trochanter and joint bones near the minimus attachment. They cannot directly confirm minimus tendon continuity or separate its injury from medius pathology.

selfCheck.question: Does selecting the minimus outline identify a separate tendon tear?
selfCheck.answer: No. This selection has no separately validated tendon segmentation or patient injury mapping.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Adducts the hip, flexes the knee and helps internally rotate the leg with the knee bent.

attachments.proximal: Pubic body and inferior pubic ramus.
attachments.distal: Proximal medial tibia within the pes anserinus.
attachments.motor: Obturator nerve; individual branching requires review.

extended.modelLimit: The supplied muscle does not separately resolve pes tendon slips or the anserine bursa. Moving it away from the knee cannot demonstrate bursitis or tendon integrity.

clinical.body: Use the level of symptoms to separate proximal adductor-region pain from distal medial-knee pain.

pathology.body: Gracilis can be involved in groin strain; its distal tendon also forms part of the pes anserinus at the medial knee.

ultrasound.body: At the tibial pes insertion, closely apposed tendons can be difficult to separate; trace the complex proximally.

ct.body: CT places the long, thin gracilis along the superficial medial thigh, separate from the deeper adductor mass. It may show a sizeable haematoma or nearby bone injury, but MRI better maps a subtle muscle injury along its length.

mri.body: MRI follows gracilis from its pubic origin through the medial thigh to the pes anserinus at the proximal tibia. Read the whole course when localising injury; medial knee change near the pes does not by itself identify a gracilis tear.

xray.body: A pelvic or knee radiograph assesses adjacent pubic or tibial bone rather than gracilis fibres. The long muscle and its pes tendon overlap other soft tissues on projection imaging, so tendon continuity cannot be inferred.

selfCheck.question: Does pes anserine bursitis prove that gracilis is torn?
selfCheck.answer: No. The adjacent bursa can be painful without a demonstrated tear in the gracilis tendon.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Flexes the hip in conjunction with psoas major.

attachments.proximal: Iliac fossa and inner iliac crest.
attachments.distal: Lesser trochanter region through the iliopsoas attachment apparatus.

extended.modelLimit: Iliacus is a separate source muscle, not a segmented iliopsoas tendon or bursa. Hip flexion, tendon excursion and the complete femoral neurovascular bundle are not simulated.

clinical.body: Hip-flexor loading can cause anterior hip symptoms. Pain, weakness and restricted movement require assessment rather than an automatic iliacus diagnosis.

pathology.body: Hip strains may affect muscle, tendon or their junction, ranging from overstretching to disruption. They are not synonymous with bursitis.

xray.body: Radiographs may be normal in snapping hip; they mainly help assess bone or joint alternatives rather than show a moving iliacus tendon.

ultrasound.body: Use the iliac wing to orient iliacus and psoas, then follow the anterior iliopsoas complex; their muscle outlines are not interchangeable.

ct.body: On CT, iliacus fills the iliac fossa and converges with psoas toward the lesser trochanter. CT helps locate a sizeable iliac-fossa collection relative to pelvic bone; it does not by itself establish subtle tendon injury.

mri.body: MRI traces iliacus from the iliac fossa into the iliopsoas complex anterior to the hip. Reviewing pelvic and proximal-thigh images helps distinguish iliacus involvement from isolated psoas or hip-joint disease.

selfCheck.question: Does moving iliacus away from psoas recreate an internal snapping hip?
selfCheck.answer: No. Explode changes viewing positions; the model has no validated tendon movement or dynamic examination.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Assists external hip rotation and abduction when the hip is flexed.

attachments.proximal: Ischial tuberosity.
attachments.distal: Medial greater trochanter through the shared obturator-internus tendon apparatus.

extended.modelLimit: The inferior gemellus remains its own source selection, not an extension of the superior gemellus. A displayed gap is not a nerve-compression site or surgical release.

clinical.body: Interpret posterior hip pain alongside lumbar, hip-joint and neurological findings.

pathology.body: The gemelli–obturator-internus region is one of several anatomical relationships considered in deep gluteal syndromes with buttock or sciatica-like pain.

ct.body: CT places the inferior gemellus immediately below the obturator internus tendon and above quadratus femoris posterior to the hip. Its small size makes separate evaluation difficult, especially without a targeted cross-sectional question.

mri.body: MRI can distinguish the inferior gemellus beside the obturator internus tendon on appropriately oriented hip images. Its relation below that tendon separates it from superior gemellus; an apparent signal change still needs correlation with the full deep gluteal region.

xray.body: Hip radiographs show the surrounding ischium, femoral head and proximal femur. They cannot distinguish inferior gemellus from obturator internus or show a small rotator injury.

ultrasound.body: Posterior hip ultrasound has a narrow, deep window to the short rotators beneath gluteus maximus. The tiny inferior gemellus lies beside the obturator internus tendon and is not reliably isolated by a general superficial scan.

selfCheck.question: Does inferior gemellus have the same usual named supply as superior gemellus?
selfCheck.answer: No. Inferior gemellus conventionally receives the nerve to quadratus femoris; superior gemellus receives the nerve to obturator internus.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Externally rotates the thigh.

attachments.proximal: External obturator membrane and adjacent bony margins.
attachments.distal: Trochanteric fossa of the femur.

extended.modelLimit: The reference surface does not show an injury grade, footprint lesion or a return-to-sport prognosis. A three-player report cannot establish general prevalence or recovery time.

clinical.body: Deep location can make the injured tissue difficult to identify from symptoms alone.

pathology.body: Obturator externus tears are uncommon reported causes of hip or groin pain. A small football-player series identified these injuries with MRI.

mri.body: MRI identified externus injuries in the cited small football-player series when symptoms overlapped with other groin injuries. The atlas is not a diagnostic scan or a recovery predictor.

ct.body: CT places obturator externus along the outer obturator membrane deep to the medial hip, passing behind the femoral neck toward the trochanteric fossa. Pelvic bone provides orientation, but MRI is more useful for a small muscle injury.

xray.body: Hip radiographs can assess the obturator-ring bones and femoral neck that frame this deep muscle. They cannot show an obturator-externus strain or distinguish externus from internus.

ultrasound.body: Obturator externus passes deep to the hip and adjacent adductors, leaving limited acoustic access. A superficial groin ultrasound cannot reliably clear its full course; targeted MRI may be needed for a suspected deep injury.

selfCheck.question: Can a three-player injury series determine every patient's recovery time?
selfCheck.answer: No. It demonstrates a reported injury pattern, not a universal prognosis or treatment protocol.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Externally rotates the hip and assists abduction with the hip flexed.

attachments.proximal: Internal obturator membrane and surrounding foramen margins.
attachments.distal: Medial greater trochanter above the trochanteric fossa.
attachments.motor: Nerve to obturator internus, not the obturator nerve.

extended.modelLimit: One supplied muscle does not separately resolve its reflected tendon, associated bursa or every gemellar connection. No nerve path is added and internus is not externus.

clinical.body: Interpret posterior hip pain alongside lumbar, hip-joint and neurological findings.

pathology.body: The gemelli–obturator-internus region is one of several anatomical relationships considered in deep gluteal syndromes with buttock or sciatica-like pain.

ct.body: CT identifies obturator internus on the inner pelvic wall and follows its tendon as it turns through the lesser sciatic notch toward the posterior hip. That reflected course distinguishes it from obturator externus; subtle tendon injury is less well defined on routine CT.

mri.body: Pelvic MRI follows the internus muscle along the obturator wall and its reflected tendon between the gemelli. The turn at the lesser sciatic notch and tendon continuity need review on the acquired planes.

xray.body: Pelvic radiographs evaluate the obturator ring and adjacent hip bones, but do not show the internus tendon turning behind the joint. A normal film does not establish that the short rotators are intact.

ultrasound.body: Posterior ultrasound may approach the short rotators below gluteus maximus, but the internus belly lies on the inner pelvic wall behind bone. The reflected tendon can be considered only in a targeted accessible window; ultrasound cannot survey the entire muscle.

selfCheck.question: Does the word obturator mean internus and externus share one nerve?
selfCheck.answer: No. Internus receives its named nerve; externus receives the obturator nerve. Similar names do not establish identical motor supply.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Adducts and flexes the thigh.

attachments.proximal: Superior pubic ramus at the pecten pubis.
attachments.distal: Femoral pectineal line.
attachments.motor: Usually femoral nerve; additional obturator supply may occur.

extended.modelLimit: This reference muscle does not map a femoral or obturator nerve branch. Typical teaching is not confirmation of this donor's variable innervation or a pain generator.

clinical.body: Its combined hip-flexion and adduction role provides context for movement-related symptoms.

pathology.body: Pectineus is one possible contributor to adductor-region injury and groin pain.

ct.body: CT locates pectineus immediately medial to iliopsoas and anterior to the deeper adductors at the proximal thigh. The pubic ramus and proximal femur orient its short course, while MRI better defines a small strain.

mri.body: On MRI, pectineus extends from the superior pubic region to the proximal femur, between iliopsoas and adductor longus. This location helps distinguish its abnormality from a deeper brevis injury or hip-joint process.

xray.body: Hip or pelvic radiographs assess nearby pubic and femoral bone. Pectineus overlaps other groin soft tissues on these views, so its fibres and tendon cannot be judged separately.

ultrasound.body: Proximal groin ultrasound can use the femoral vessels and iliopsoas as orientation before moving medially to pectineus. Its short, deep course and neighbouring adductors require careful two-plane tracing; one superficial view cannot exclude an injury.

selfCheck.question: Do all medial-thigh adductors share only obturator supply?
selfCheck.answer: No. Pectineus usually receives femoral supply, sometimes with additional obturator contribution; the donor's precise branches are not mapped.

motorGroups.caveat: Usual supply; variable obturator/accessory obturator contributions are not separately mapped.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Everts the foot, assists ankle plantarflexion and supports the transverse arch.

attachments.proximal: Fibular head and proximal lateral shaft, with septal attachments.
attachments.distal: Plantar first-metatarsal base and medial cuneiform, after crossing the sole.

extended.modelLimit: The source calls this peroneus longus (fibularis longus). Brevis, retinacula, os peroneum and tendon-sheath disease are not separate validated selections; separation is not tendon subluxation.

clinical.body: Relate eversion and first-ray support to the longus tendon course.

pathology.body: Fibularis longus tendon disease can cause lateral ankle or plantar-lateral foot pain.

mri.body: MRI can assess the peroneal tendons and surrounding tissues for tears or inflammation. Findings must distinguish longus from brevis rather than assigning all lateral pain to longus.

ultrasound.body: Dynamic ultrasound can examine peroneal tendon movement and instability. Evidence from a selected surgical cohort does not establish universal accuracy; this static mesh cannot reproduce a dynamic examination.

ct.body: CT defines lateral-malleolar and cuboid bone relationships along the fibularis-longus tendon path. Soft-tissue windows may give context but are not a routine tendon-continuity examination. This selection does not include a separately validated brevis tendon.

xray.body: Ankle and foot radiographs assess lateral bony injury and an os peroneum when present. They do not directly show a peroneus-longus tendon tear or dynamic subluxation. Retinacular competence is not inferred from this static model.

selfCheck.question: Does separation of this surface demonstrate peroneal tendon instability?
selfCheck.answer: No. Explode mode only changes presentation; it contains no validated retinaculum, tendon tracking or dynamic scan.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Assists external hip rotation and abduction of the flexed thigh.

attachments.proximal: Pelvic surface of the sacrum, with variable adjacent attachments.
attachments.distal: Superior aspect of the greater trochanter.
attachments.motor: Nerve to piriformis from the sacral plexus; branching varies.

extended.modelLimit: The piriformis surface cannot establish a through-muscle sciatic variant, entrapment or the diagnostic performance of a provocative test. No missing sciatic nerve is fabricated.

clinical.body: Use this muscle for regional orientation while considering the wider clinical differential.

pathology.body: Piriformis-related sciatic irritation is a possible explanation for some buttock and radiating leg pain.

mri.body: Pelvic MRI may help investigate deep gluteal causes after considering spinal disease. A piriformis selection does not prove nerve entrapment.

ct.body: CT places piriformis from the anterior sacrum through the greater sciatic foramen toward the greater trochanter. It can locate a large deep-gluteal collection or adjacent bone abnormality, but cannot determine nerve entrapment from muscle size alone.

xray.body: Pelvic radiographs show sacral and hip bone alignment around piriformis but do not display the muscle or sciatic nerve separately. They cannot establish or exclude a piriformis-related neuropathy.

ultrasound.body: Piriformis lies deep to gluteus maximus near the posterior hip, so ultrasound access varies with depth and habitus. A targeted examination may orient to the greater sciatic notch, but cannot survey its sacral origin or prove sciatic entrapment.

selfCheck.question: Does the atlas demonstrate sciatic entrapment within this piriformis?
selfCheck.answer: No. It shows the source muscle, not a mapped sciatic variant, compression site or patient-specific lesion.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Flexes the hip; with the femur fixed, contributes to movement and support of the lumbar region.

attachments.proximal: Lower thoracic/lumbar vertebral bodies and discs, and lumbar transverse processes.
attachments.distal: Lesser trochanter through the iliopsoas tendon apparatus.
attachments.motor: Direct branches of lumbar anterior rami, not the femoral supply of iliacus.

extended.modelLimit: The psoas surface is not a lumbar-plexus, tendon-sheath or retroperitoneal disease model. Neither internal snapping nor nerve compression can be diagnosed from its shape.

clinical.body: Anterior snapping may involve the iliopsoas tendon, but snapping can also arise outside or within the hip joint.

pathology.body: A moving tendon can be associated with bursal irritation. Labral or cartilage problems can also cause catching, so these mechanisms must not be conflated.

xray.body: A radiograph may help investigate bony alternatives but does not directly demonstrate the transient tendon movement causing a snap.

ultrasound.body: The iliopsoas tendon is deep within the anterior muscle complex; its bursa lies between tendon and anterior capsule, normally collapsed.

ct.body: CT follows psoas major beside the lumbar spine and across the pelvic brim toward the iliopsoas tendon. This retroperitoneal location is important when assessing a collection or mass, but CT findings need the full clinical context and do not establish a muscle-specific cause of hip pain.

mri.body: MRI can trace psoas major from the lumbar vertebrae to its confluence with iliacus near the lesser trochanter. Coronal and axial coverage helps separate a psoas process from iliacus, spine or hip disease.

selfCheck.question: Is every catch or click inside the hip caused by iliopsoas?
selfCheck.answer: No. Tendons at other locations and intra-articular cartilage or labral problems can produce mechanical symptoms.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Externally rotates the thigh.

attachments.proximal: Lateral border of the ischial tuberosity.
attachments.distal: Posterior proximal femur at the quadrate line near the intertrochanteric crest.

extended.modelLimit: Neither the ischiofemoral space nor quadratus femoris signal is clinically measured here. Display separation changes spacing without simulating impingement or decompression.

clinical.body: Interpret suspected impingement with symptoms, examination and imaging position rather than a single space measurement.

pathology.body: Ischiofemoral impingement involves the quadratus femoris region between the ischium and lesser trochanter.

mri.body: Ischiofemoral asymmetry, fatty change and oedema were observed in some asymptomatic volunteers. MRI findings and spacing alone do not establish symptomatic impingement.

ct.body: CT locates quadratus femoris between the ischial tuberosity and posterior proximal femur, below the gemelli and obturator internus. The nearby ischiofemoral interval is positional; a narrow interval alone does not establish symptomatic impingement.

xray.body: Hip radiographs assess the ischium and proximal femur forming this region. They cannot directly show quadratus-femoris oedema or turn a projected bone interval into a muscle diagnosis.

ultrasound.body: Quadratus femoris is a deep, flat short rotator beneath gluteus maximus between the ischium and femur. Its depth and overlying tissues limit ultrasound assessment; a superficial normal scan cannot clear its whole belly.

selfCheck.question: Does ischiofemoral asymmetry on MRI necessarily explain hip pain?
selfCheck.answer: No. Asymmetry and some signal changes occur without symptoms; correlate findings with the clinical assessment and imaging position.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Assists toe flexion through the long-flexor tendon, rather than a direct attachment to a toe bone.

attachments.proximal: Medial calcaneus and lateral calcaneal tuberosity.
attachments.distal: Flexor digitorum longus tendon apparatus.

extended.modelLimit: The supplied muscle is not separated into two validated head selections or individual FDL attachment slips. No lateral plantar nerve path or denervation pattern is modelled.

clinical.body: Quadratus plantae assists flexion through the long-flexor tendon apparatus, rather than attaching directly to a toe phalanx.

pathology.body: Lateral plantar motor dysfunction may involve quadratus plantae alongside other intrinsic muscles.

ct.body: CT shows plantar bone context but is not the preferred study for a suspected small intrinsic-muscle lesion. MRI or targeted ultrasound may be chosen after an unresolved soft-tissue question. This source surface is not a two-head or nerve map.

mri.body: MRI places quadratus plantae deep to FDB and beside the long-flexor tendon apparatus. Assess any signal change with the wider plantar layers and clinical question. It does not insert directly on a toe phalanx.

xray.body: Foot radiographs show bones and alignment overlying the deep plantar muscle. They cannot depict quadratus-plantae fibres or determine lateral-plantar nerve function. No individual head is identified by this mesh.

ultrasound.body: A plantar ultrasound approach may reach quadratus plantae beneath FDB, but depth and overlying tissue limit detail. Trace the deeper muscle and FDL relation rather than calling the superficial FDB quadratus plantae. This is not a nerve-conduction test.

selfCheck.question: Does quadratus plantae attach directly to a toe phalanx?
selfCheck.answer: No. Its contribution is through the long-flexor tendon apparatus, not a direct phalangeal insertion.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Extends the knee and flexes the hip; unlike the vasti, it crosses both joints.

attachments.proximal: Anterior inferior iliac spine and the region above the acetabular rim through direct and indirect tendons.
attachments.distal: Patella through the quadriceps tendon; force continues through the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.

extended.modelLimit: The muscle surface does not separately segment direct/reflected tendons or central aponeurosis. This adult specimen cannot show an adolescent growth-plate avulsion.

clinical.body: Acute anterior-thigh pain during rapid activity can reflect muscle injury. Examine the hip, knee and extensor apparatus rather than localising by pain alone.

pathology.body: Muscle injury may involve the belly or muscle-tendon junction. Partial disruption and complete tendon detachment are different injuries.

mri.body: MRI can characterize muscle and tendon injury when needed, including whether a suspected strain involves a more substantial tendon lesion.

xray.body: Radiographs assess suspected bone injury; an unremarkable film does not establish that the rectus muscle-tendon unit is intact.

ultrasound.body: The direct proximal tendon relates to the anterior inferior iliac spine; deeper central aponeurotic anatomy differs from the superficial tendon contribution.

ct.body: CT identifies rectus femoris in the superficial central anterior thigh, anterior to the vasti, and can assess adjacent pelvic bone near its origin. MRI or targeted ultrasound is better for defining a muscle or proximal tendon injury.

selfCheck.question: Can this single muscle surface show which proximal rectus tendon has torn?
selfCheck.answer: No. Its tendon components are not separate validated selections; imaging and clinical review would be needed.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Flexes, abducts and externally rotates the hip; flexes the knee and assists internal leg rotation when it is bent.

attachments.proximal: Anterior superior iliac spine.
attachments.distal: Proximal medial tibia within the pes anserinus.

extended.modelLimit: One source muscle does not separately segment the anserine bursa or individual pes insertion footprints. The model cannot assess passive flexibility or reproduce medial-knee pain.

clinical.body: Localise symptoms relative to the joint line and consider competing knee causes.

pathology.body: Distal sartorius participates in the pes anserinus, beside a bursa that can become a source of medial-knee pain.

ultrasound.body: Posteromedial knee ultrasound distinguishes sartorius muscle from nearby gracilis and semitendinosus tendons before their closely apposed insertion.

ct.body: CT follows sartorius as a superficial strap from the anterior superior iliac spine obliquely across the anterior thigh toward the medial knee. Its long course helps orient the femoral triangle and adductor canal; subtle strain needs dedicated soft-tissue assessment.

mri.body: MRI can trace sartorius along its oblique anterior-thigh course to the medial proximal tibia. Review the proximal muscle and distal pes region separately; a medial-knee finding need not involve the entire muscle.

xray.body: Pelvic, femoral or knee radiographs may show bone injury near either sartorius attachment. They cannot follow the oblique muscle itself or establish pes tendon integrity.

selfCheck.question: Does sharing the pes insertion make sartorius a hamstring?
selfCheck.answer: No. Sartorius is a femoral-supplied anterior-thigh muscle; sharing an insertion does not make these muscles anatomically identical.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Extends the hip, flexes the knee and assists internal leg rotation with the knee bent.

attachments.proximal: Ischial tuberosity.
attachments.distal: Posterior aspect of the medial tibial condyle, with associated tendon expansions.
attachments.motor: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve.

extended.modelLimit: One muscle surface is supplied, without separate tendon expansions, tear margins or measured retraction. Its medial distal anatomy should not be replaced with a biceps-femoris label.

clinical.body: Localise this medial hamstring separately from lateral biceps femoris. Their distal attachments differ even though both contribute to knee flexion.

pathology.body: Hamstring injury can affect muscle or tendon; severe proximal injury may detach tendon from the ischial origin.

mri.body: MRI helps characterize hamstring soft-tissue injury and its severity; the atlas itself has no tear map.

xray.body: Radiographs can demonstrate a bony avulsion but do not directly establish hamstring soft-tissue continuity.

ultrasound.body: The ischial tuberosity orients the proximal hamstrings. Closely adjacent tendon origins may be difficult to separate; avoid assigning an unverified individual footprint.

ct.body: CT places semimembranosus in the deep medial posterior thigh from the ischium toward the posteromedial tibia. It can locate a large collection or bony avulsion, while MRI better distinguishes its tendon from adjacent semitendinosus.

selfCheck.question: Does an apparent gap created by dissection demonstrate tendon retraction?
selfCheck.answer: No. It is a reversible viewing arrangement, not measured traumatic displacement or a patient finding.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Extends the hip, flexes the knee and assists internal leg rotation with the knee bent.

attachments.proximal: Ischial tuberosity.
attachments.distal: Proximal medial tibia within the pes anserinus.
attachments.motor: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve.

extended.modelLimit: Semitendinosus remains distinct from semimembranosus. The pes anserinus and proximal shared tendon are not separately segmented or a complete graft-harvest simulation.

clinical.body: Its long distal tendon reaches the medial tibia through the pes anserinus. Do not confuse this with semimembranosus insertion.

pathology.body: Overload can injure hamstring muscle or tendon; severe avulsion is different from a mild muscle strain.

mri.body: MRI can assess the extent of a hamstring injury rather than infer severity from visible bruising alone.

xray.body: A tendon avulsion may pull off bone visible on a radiograph; an absent fragment does not prove tendon integrity.

ct.body: CT follows semitendinosus in the medial posterior thigh, superficial to semimembranosus, ending in a long pes tendon. It may locate a large injury or collection, but MRI better resolves proximal tendon and muscle extent.

ultrasound.body: Posteromedial knee ultrasound can follow the slender semitendinosus tendon toward the pes anserinus and compare it with deeper semimembranosus. Proximal hamstring origin is much deeper, so a distal scan cannot establish its integrity.

selfCheck.question: Does semitendinosus share the lateral fibular attachment of biceps femoris?
selfCheck.answer: No. Semitendinosus reaches the medial tibia through the pes anserinus, whereas biceps femoris attaches laterally.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Plantarflexes the ankle. Unlike gastrocnemius, it does not cross the knee.

attachments.proximal: Posterior proximal fibula and tibial soleal-line region.
attachments.distal: Posterior calcaneus through the shared calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.

extended.modelLimit: The supplied soleus has no segmented intramuscular aponeuroses, strain grades or pressure compartments. Its separation from gastrocnemius is neither a tear nor a surgical decompression.

clinical.body: Soleus crosses the ankle, not the knee; bending the knee changes gastrocnemius length without turning movement into a perfectly isolated soleus test.

pathology.body: Soleus strain and injury to the shared Achilles apparatus can both affect calf loading, but they are not the same lesion.

mri.body: MRI can localise soleus injury when a deeper lesion is not adequately shown by ultrasound. The referenced study used MRI as its comparison standard, not this atlas surface.

ultrasound.body: A negative ultrasound does not reliably exclude a soleus injury. Deeper lesions were missed in the referenced clinical series; image quality, lesion location and the clinical question matter.

ct.body: CT gives bone context around the deep calf, but MRI has been used to characterise injuries within the calf muscle complex. This soleus surface does not segment an intramuscular lesion or measure compartment pressure. A bone-focused CT view cannot supply those findings.

xray.body: Leg radiographs assess tibial or fibular bone injury around soleus. They do not show a deeper soleus strain or exclude one. The two gastrocnemius heads remain separate overlying structures.

selfCheck.question: Does a normal ultrasound necessarily exclude a deeper soleus strain?
selfCheck.answer: No. Ultrasound missed lesions in the referenced series; clinical assessment determines whether further investigation is needed.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Assists external hip rotation and abduction when the hip is flexed.

attachments.proximal: Ischial spine.
attachments.distal: Medial greater trochanter through the shared obturator-internus tendon apparatus.

extended.modelLimit: The supplied superior gemellus is separate from the inferior gemellus. No sciatic entrapment site, nerve variant or muscle-specific provocative test is demonstrated.

clinical.body: Interpret posterior hip pain alongside lumbar, hip-joint and neurological findings.

pathology.body: The gemelli–obturator-internus region is one of several anatomical relationships considered in deep gluteal syndromes with buttock or sciatica-like pain.

ct.body: CT locates superior gemellus at the posterior hip just above the obturator internus tendon, near the ischial spine. It helps orient the deep rotator layer, but the small muscle may be difficult to separate from its neighbours on routine CT.

mri.body: On hip MRI, follow the short rotator layer from the ischial spine toward the greater trochanter; superior gemellus lies above the obturator internus tendon. Its position, not the shared tendon region alone, distinguishes it from inferior gemellus.

xray.body: Hip radiographs assess neighbouring pelvic and femoral bone. Projection overlap prevents identification of the superior gemellus or its distinction from the obturator internus tendon.

ultrasound.body: A posterior ultrasound approach must look through gluteus maximus toward the deep rotators. Superior gemellus is small and closely apposed to obturator internus, so an isolated normal finding is difficult to establish sonographically.

selfCheck.question: Which named nerve typically supplies superior gemellus?
selfCheck.answer: The nerve to obturator internus. This conventional relationship is not a reconstruction of the source donor's nerve branches.

motorGroups.caveat: Additional supply from the nerve to quadratus femoris is reported.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Assists hip flexion, abduction and internal rotation while tensioning the iliotibial tract.

attachments.proximal: Anterior iliac crest near the anterior superior iliac spine.
attachments.distal: Iliotibial tract; its distal continuation reaches the lateral proximal tibia.

extended.modelLimit: The source muscle does not include a separately validated iliotibial tract or bursa. It is not connected to the tibia by a newly invented direct tendon; no snapping motion is simulated.

clinical.body: Distinguish external lateral snapping from anterior iliopsoas-related snapping or an intra-articular problem.

pathology.body: The iliotibial tract can contribute to external snapping over the greater trochanter, sometimes with lateral hip discomfort.

ultrasound.body: Lateral hip ultrasound places the fascia lata superficial to gluteal tissues and the greater trochanter. This muscle-only selection cannot depict fascial snapping.

ct.body: CT places tensor fasciae latae in the anterolateral proximal thigh between the iliac crest region and iliotibial tract. It can orient a large lateral soft-tissue abnormality, but MRI better defines a small muscle injury.

mri.body: MRI follows the short muscle from the anterior iliac crest toward the iliotibial tract, separate from the deeper gluteus medius. Lateral hip symptoms require assessment of both the muscle and adjacent abductor tendons; one selection does not identify the pain source.

xray.body: Pelvic and hip radiographs show the nearby iliac crest and greater trochanteric bone. They do not directly depict tensor fasciae latae or the length of the iliotibial tract.

selfCheck.question: Does external hip snapping mean TFL itself has torn?
selfCheck.answer: No. Snapping can involve the iliotibial tract and may be painless; a snap alone does not establish a muscle tear.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Dorsiflexes the ankle and inverts the foot, helping clear the toes during swing.

attachments.proximal: Lateral tibial condyle, proximal lateral shaft and interosseous membrane.
attachments.distal: Medial cuneiform and first-metatarsal base.

extended.modelLimit: This muscle reference is not a torn tendon or a mapped neurological lesion. It contains no motor testing, gait simulation or measured compartment pressure.

clinical.body: Assess ankle dorsiflexion and inversion alongside toe extension, sensation and gait.

pathology.body: Tibialis-anterior tendon disease or rupture can impair dorsiflexion. Foot drop can also arise from nerve, root or other neurological disease.

mri.body: Assess the tibialis anterior tendon together with its extensor-retinacular relationship. A small cadaver/patient study correlated standard and oblique-coronal MRI with this anatomy; its tear patterns are not universal diagnostic rules. The specimen does not separately segment those retinacular tunnels or patient injury.

ultrasound.body: Follow tibialis anterior from its muscle-tendon junction across the anterior ankle towards its medial insertion. Inspect beyond a single transverse view; the specimen does not provide ultrasound images.

ct.body: CT shows anterior tibial and ankle bone relationships along the tibialis-anterior path. It is not a routine test of tendon continuity or dorsiflexion strength. The mesh does not include a measured compartment pressure.

xray.body: Leg and ankle films assess osseous injury adjacent to tibialis anterior. They cannot directly establish tendon rupture or distinguish tendon injury from a neurological cause of foot drop. Clinical localisation remains necessary.

selfCheck.question: Is foot drop a diagnosis of tibialis-anterior tendon rupture?
selfCheck.answer: No. It describes impaired dorsiflexion with several possible muscular, tendon and neurological causes.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Inverts the foot, assists plantarflexion and supports the medial longitudinal arch.

attachments.proximal: Posterior tibia, fibula and intervening interosseous membrane.
attachments.distal: Main attachment at the navicular tuberosity, with expansions to cuneiforms and other plantar midfoot sites.

extended.modelLimit: The muscle surface does not separately resolve every insertion slip or the ligament support of the arch. Reference bone spacing is not a weight-bearing deformity measurement.

clinical.body: Medial ankle/arch symptoms, standing alignment and heel-rise function help assess the posterior tibial apparatus.

pathology.body: Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction can contribute to progressive collapsing foot deformity.

mri.body: MRI may assess posterior tibial tendon and associated ligament abnormalities when needed. Progressive arch collapse is not necessarily an isolated muscle lesion.

xray.body: Standing radiographs assess alignment and joint changes under load. They do not directly show tendon continuity; rotating or exploding this model is not a weight-bearing radiograph.

ultrasound.body: Trace tibialis posterior behind the medial malleolus towards its insertion, distinguishing adjacent FDL. Examine the navicular insertion region separately; this specimen does not resolve every distal tendon slip.

ct.body: CT defines the medial-malleolar and midfoot bone relationships crossed by tibialis posterior. It may clarify an associated bony abnormality, but not every distal tendon slip or arch-support ligament. This static reference is not a standing alignment study.

selfCheck.question: Can exploded arch spacing grade progressive collapsing foot deformity?
selfCheck.answer: No. Display spacing is not a calibrated standing alignment study and the full ligament apparatus is absent.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Extends the knee as part of the quadriceps; it does not cross the hip.

attachments.proximal: Anterior and lateral femoral shaft.
attachments.distal: Patella through the quadriceps tendon; force continues through the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.

extended.modelLimit: The deep vastus remains a whole muscle surface without separate intramuscular laminae or tendon-layer injury grades. Rectus femoris is a different selectable muscle above it.

clinical.body: Assess extension through the complete quadriceps apparatus; selecting this deep muscle does not isolate its force contribution.

pathology.body: A quadriceps-tendon tear disrupts force transmission to the patella. Complete disruption can cause major loss of active knee extension.

ultrasound.body: The conventional deep quadriceps-tendon layer relates to intermedius; a muscle surface does not resolve tendon-layer tears.

ct.body: CT places vastus intermedius directly anterior to the femoral shaft beneath rectus femoris. It can define a large deep anterior-thigh collection, but MRI better separates a subtle intermedius injury from adjacent quadriceps heads.

mri.body: MRI tracks vastus intermedius along the anterior femur into the shared quadriceps tendon. Its deep position beneath rectus femoris is the key localising feature; tendon findings must be assessed with the entire extensor apparatus.

xray.body: Femoral or knee radiographs assess adjacent bone and patellar alignment. They cannot isolate the deep intermedius from rectus femoris or demonstrate its fibre integrity.

selfCheck.question: Does vastus intermedius cross the hip like rectus femoris?
selfCheck.answer: No. The vasti arise from the femur and act across the knee; rectus femoris also crosses the hip.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Extends the knee as part of the quadriceps; it does not cross the hip.

attachments.proximal: Greater trochanter, gluteal tuberosity and lateral lip of the femoral linea aspera.
attachments.distal: Patella through the quadriceps tendon; force continues through the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.

extended.modelLimit: One lateral vastus surface does not include a separately resolved lateral retinaculum or injury to the shared tendon. Dissection movement is not patellar tracking.

clinical.body: Vastus lateralis contributes to knee extension with the other quadriceps muscles. Weakness alone does not isolate a lateral-vastus lesion.

pathology.body: A quadriceps-tendon tear disrupts force transmission to the patella. Complete disruption can cause major loss of active knee extension.

ultrasound.body: Lateralis contributes to the conventional intermediate quadriceps-tendon layer with medialis; ultrasound assessment follows the shared apparatus.

ct.body: CT places vastus lateralis along the lateral femoral shaft, deep to the iliotibial tract and beside the other quadriceps heads. It can show a large collection or associated femoral injury, while MRI better assesses a subtle fibre lesion.

mri.body: MRI follows vastus lateralis along the lateral femur into the quadriceps tendon. Its position separates it from rectus femoris anteriorly and the deeper vastus intermedius; a focal injury should be localised within the acquired planes.

xray.body: Femur or knee radiographs assess underlying bone and alignment near the lateral quadriceps. They cannot resolve the lateral muscle belly or prove tendon continuity.

selfCheck.question: Can this muscle-only selection establish continuity of the whole quadriceps tendon?
selfCheck.answer: No. It is a source muscle surface, not an examination of the separately supplied tendon or all of its layers.

lesson.anatomy: Typical attachments are described below. Their footprints, tendon subdivisions and motor territories are not mapped on this specimen.
lesson.function: Extends the knee as part of the quadriceps; it does not cross the hip.

attachments.proximal: Intertrochanteric line and medial lip of the femoral linea aspera.
attachments.distal: Patella through the quadriceps tendon; force continues through the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.

extended.modelLimit: No separately validated VMO/VML subdivision, medial retinaculum or maltracking mechanism is supplied. A whole-muscle label must not be promoted to a fibre-specific treatment target.

clinical.body: Assess medialis within the extensor mechanism. This whole-muscle selection cannot quantify isolated fibre recruitment or establish patellar tracking.

pathology.body: A quadriceps-tendon tear disrupts force transmission to the patella. Complete disruption can cause major loss of active knee extension.

ultrasound.body: Medialis joins lateralis in the conventional intermediate tendon layer; this whole muscle does not identify isolated VMO pathology.

ct.body: CT locates vastus medialis along the medial femoral shaft and distal medial knee, adjacent to the other quadriceps heads. A large collection may be visible, but MRI better defines a focal muscle injury or its distal extent.

mri.body: MRI follows vastus medialis into the medial quadriceps expansion near the patella. Its medial position helps distinguish it from rectus femoris and intermedius; a distal finding needs assessment with the rest of the extensor mechanism.

xray.body: Femoral and knee radiographs show bone and patellar alignment, not separate vastus-medialis fibres. Patellar position alone cannot establish whether this muscle is weak or torn.

selfCheck.question: Does the atlas contain a separately validated VMO selection?
selfCheck.answer: No. It retains the supplied whole vastus medialis surface, without an inferred fibre-specific compartment.

lesson.anatomy: Calcaneal tendon shared principally by gastrocnemius and soleus.
lesson.function: Transmits plantarflexion force to the calcaneus.

extended.modelLimit: This surface does not separately map gastrocnemius/soleus subtendons, perfusion zones or a tear gap. Separation is not dorsiflexion or a dynamic tendon test.

clinical.body: Sudden posterior ankle pain or a pop with reduced push-off raises concern for rupture. Clinicians assess tendon continuity and the calf-squeeze response alongside the history.

pathology.body: Rupture may be partial or complete and occur within the tendon or at its calcaneal attachment. Tendon degeneration and traumatic disruption are not synonymous.

mri.body: MRI can assess tear extent and location and identify alternative soft-tissue causes of symptoms.

xray.body: Insertional avulsion may leave a small calcaneal fragment visible on radiographs. Absence of a fragment does not establish tendon continuity.

ultrasound.body: Ultrasound can show tendon continuity and changes with ankle movement in real time. This atlas is static source geometry, not a dynamic scan or tendon-gap measurement.

ct.body: CT can define a calcaneal avulsion or other bone injury at the Achilles insertion. It is not the usual direct assessment of tendon fibre continuity compared with ultrasound or MRI. This intact source tendon cannot establish plantarflexion strength or a patient rupture.

selfCheck.question: Does a normal bone radiograph exclude Achilles rupture?
selfCheck.answer: No. A tendon can rupture without an avulsed bone fragment.
